# The Slowest Conversation on Earth

Somewhere near you, probably within a few hundred feet, a very old argument is taking place on a rock.

It looks like nothing much: a crust of pale green, or a smear of orange on a stone wall, or a gray-blue frill on a tree branch. Most people walk past lichens their entire lives without registering them as alive, let alone as one of the stranger things alive. They get mistaken for moss, for mold, for stains, for the ordinary grime of old surfaces. But a lichen is not a single organism at all. It is a relationship that learned to take a shape.

For most of scientific history, nobody knew this. Lichens were classified as plants, sorted and named and pressed into herbaria like any other plant. Then in 1867, a Swiss botanist named Simon Schwendener proposed something that struck his colleagues as absurd: that a lichen was really two organisms, a fungus and an alga, living as one. The fungus builds the structure, the body, the architecture that clings to the rock and holds water. The alga, tucked inside, photosynthesizes and feeds the whole enterprise sugar.

The reaction was hostile. Prominent lichenologists called the idea a "romance" and a fiction. Some of the resistance was simply the ordinary inertia of a field that had spent careers describing lichens as unified beings. But some of it seemed almost philosophical. An organism was supposed to be a *thing*, bounded and singular. The idea that a living creature might be a negotiated arrangement between two unrelated kingdoms of life felt like a category error, as if someone had claimed that a marriage was a person.

The dual hypothesis won, eventually. The word "symbiosis," in its biological sense, emerged partly to describe what was happening in lichens. Beatrix Potter, before she became famous for rabbits in waistcoats, was a serious mycologist who studied fungi and supported the idea that lichens were dual organisms; her paper on spore germination had to be read aloud at the Linnean Society by a man, because women were not permitted to attend. The history of lichens is threaded through with this sort of thing: truths sitting in plain sight, waiting for the right people to be allowed to say them.

And then, in 2016, the story turned over again. Researchers led by Toby Spribille found that many lichens contain a *third* partner: a yeast, living in the outer layer, that had been overlooked for nearly 150 years because nobody thought to look for it. The two-body problem was a three-body problem. Some lichens seem to involve even more participants, bacterial communities that may contribute something to the whole. The lichen is less a duet than a small town.

What I find moving about this is how it unsettles the idea of the individual. We like to think of living things as discrete units, each with its own boundaries and its own interests. But the lichen suggests that "individual" may sometimes be a word for a stable pattern of cooperation that lasts long enough to be recognized. A lichen has a species name, a characteristic shape and color, a predictable way of growing. It reproduces, sometimes by releasing little packets that contain both fungus and alga together, a partnership traveling as a unit. By almost every practical measure, it behaves like one thing. And yet it is not one thing. It is an agreement.

Humans are not so different, it turns out. We carry trillions of microbes, and our cells contain mitochondria that were once, very long ago, free-living bacteria that took up residence and never left. The lichen is just unusually honest about it. It wears its partnership on the outside.

Then there is the matter of time. Lichens are slow in a way that is hard to hold in the mind. Some species grow less than a millimeter a year. The map lichen, *Rhizocarpon geographicum*, which spreads across rocks in yellow-green patches outlined in black like countries on an atlas, grows so slowly and so steadily that geologists use it as a clock. By measuring the diameter of lichen patches on stones left behind by retreating glaciers, they can estimate how long ago the ice pulled away. This technique is called lichenometry, and it relies on the fact that a lichen, once established, simply keeps going, adding its fractions of a millimeter year after year, through wars and plagues and the rise and fall of languages. Some Arctic lichens are thought to be thousands of years old. A patch you could cover with your palm might have begun growing before anyone wrote anything down.

This slowness is also a kind of toughness. Lichens colonize places almost nothing else can: bare rock, desert crusts, Antarctic stone, tombstones, rooftops. Many of them can dry out completely and suspend their metabolism, waiting, sometimes for long stretches, until water returns. In 2005, the European Space Agency sent lichens into orbit and exposed them to the vacuum of space, to cosmic radiation and ultraviolet light, for about fifteen days. When they came back, they resumed normal activity. They had, in effect, shrugged.

And yet they are fragile in one specific way: many lichens are exquisitely sensitive to air pollution, especially sulfur dioxide. Because they absorb nearly everything they need directly from the air and rain, they have no way to filter out what's poisonous. During the Industrial Revolution, lichens vanished from the trees around English cities. Their return, in recent decades, has been one of the quieter signs that the air got cleaner. You can read the health of a place partly by what is growing on its stones.

I like to think about all of this when I look at a weathered wall or an old gravestone. The orange blotch there is not decoration or decay. It is a partnership among at least two, maybe three, maybe many forms of life, each unable to do alone what they manage together. It has been keeping time at a pace far slower than ours, patiently turning rock into soil one molecule at a time, making the first ground that other things will someday grow in.

It asks nothing of us. It will probably outlast the wall. And it offers, to anyone who stops long enough to look, a small, strange lesson: that being a self might sometimes mean being a conversation that has learned to hold still.

message.reasoning:
I'm brainstorming an interesting topic to write about — considering maps that distort truth, the history of blue as a color, tide pools, endangered languages, old handwriting, before deciding the ship of Theseus and petrichor feel too familiar and looking for something fresher.

Actually, lichens feel like the right choice: their strange symbiotic partnership, glacial slowness, and use in dating rocks give me room to reflect on identity without being heavy-handed. I'm gathering facts to ground the essay — the fungus-alga partnership, the 2016 discovery of a third yeast partner, Schwendener's derided dual hypothesis, Beatrix Potter's overlooked contributions, and lichenometry using map lichens to date ancient glacial moraines.

I'm also noting the 2005 ESA space survival experiment, lichens' coverage of the land surface, their role as reindeer food and pollution indicators, and the coinage of "symbiosis" itself in a lichen context. Time to write it.
